incidents.incident_description: (approx.. 12/15/2022) The consumer was pre-heating the oven, but when she checked it 20 minutes later, it was still on the “pre-heat” setting and the oven was cold. She turned it off and stopped using it. A few days later, her girlfriend suggested that they simply re-light the oven pilot. They unscrewed the metal plate at the bottom of the oven. There was a tunnel underneath the oven and that tunnel area was filled with small metal pieces. (12/2022) The consumer called a local service company, (Chucks Appliances), and a rep. named [REDACTED], came over and examined the oven. He removed the same parts and saw the same pieces. He told the consumer that the oven’s ignition did not work and those metal pieces may be a factor or the cause of the issue. [REDACTED] asked for a magnet and when the consumer gave him one, the pieces inside the oven tunnel were found to be magnetic. [REDACTED] also said that it was unknown if those metal pieces, which seemed to break off a metal plate in that area of the oven, may have gotten in the consumer’s food, when cooking. A few days later, the consumer called the dealer and reported the problem to their rep. (name unavailable). The rep. told her the manufacturer would not do anything because the oven was out of warranty. However, he asked the consumer to send photos, which she did and he forwarded them onto his manager, who sent them to the manufacturer. The manufacturer responded and offered her 30% off the purchase of a new one. The consumer declined this offer due to her safety concerns and said she doesn’t even want another one of their products. Lastly, the oven door glass has a thin piece of silver insulation that is kitty-corner on 1 end and part of that metal insulation is starting to corrode. This also adds to her safety concerns.

incidents.incident_description: On Saturday, January 28, 2023 at approximately 10:30 a.m., I unplugged my Conair 1875 hairdryer from the outlet and next thing I remember - I was flat on my back and had blacked out for a few seconds......I didn't know what happened. I thought maybe when I bent over to unplug it - I thought maybe I got light-headed and passed out. I have never passed out before in my life (I am 57 years old). Later in the evening - I was getting ready to go out and again I plugged in my hair dryer (I use it to heat up my eyelash curler) and this time when I went to unplug it - I squatted down so that I didn't lean over and pull the plug out. Next thing I know - i was on my back again and I had blacked out for a few seconds. My 85-year old mother and my sister both heard me fall on the floor....at that time - I still didn't know what happened. Then I realized that I had blacked out and fallen both times that day at the exact same time that I was unplugging that hairdryer. I had an electrician come out on January 30th and he said there wasn't anything wrong with the actual outlet and it had to be the hairdryer plug that was the problem. I have a black eye from the fall (I don't know if the black eye is from me pulling the plug out and possibly hitting myself in the eye when I got electrocuted or I don't know if the electrical current went in through my eye. All I know is that it was a scary situation and I am worried about my heart. I already have a rapid heart beat (supraventricular tachycardia) and I am lucky that I didn't actually die from being shocked twice in one day.

I scooted the shattered dish and chicken resting on the wire rack into a metal pan. I let the rest of the mess and oven cool before continuing with the cleanup. I took 4 pictures. incidents.company_comment: (4/21/2023) Delta Faucet Company: Liberty has reached out to this consumer to gather more details in order to fully investigate this report. While Liberty regrets that the consumer had this experience, it does not believe the shower doors it sells pose a significant consumer risk, notwithstanding the fact that because they are glass, they may be broken during the course of use. Tempered glass doors are extremely strong and are commonly used in bathrooms in place of shower curtains. These doors are made to the strict standards of ANSI Z97.1 and CPSC regulations for architectural glass found at 16 CFR part 1201. The tempering process creates stresses on the glass that allow the glass to withstand greater than normal forces on its surface. Tempered glass, although extremely strong, can break if an end or corner is scratched, damaged, or impacted – these types of things can occur when the glass shower door unit is not installed as directed in the instructions provided with the product at the time of sale. It is uncommon for tempered glass to break, but when it happens, the glass does not splinter into jagged shards; rather, it breaks into small granular chunks to minimize risk to nearby people and property. Liberty takes product safety seriously and encourages all consumers to reach out to share information regarding product performance.

She woke up in the middle of the night to the home filled with smoke. The mother went to the kitchen and there were flames and smoke shooting from the dishwasher. She used her cell phone to call the fire department. The fire department came and extinguished the fire, but there was extensive damage to the home resulting from the fire. incidents.incident_description: The Apple iPhone 15 pro max titanium is dangerously defective. It emits a constant low voltage electrical current constantly even when not connected to a charger, but also when in use. It is measurable with a multimeter and an oscilloscope. I have personally had more than one of these devices that have done this, and there are (after some light research) similar complaints online and in my social circle. When in use it give a constant oscillating voltage that is passed into points of contact, such as your hands. It starts as a tingle or pulsing, which turns uncomfortable the longer you use it. It causes discomfort and tingling, either stinging or numbness during short term use like a phone call, and when used longer it leads to muscle contractions, a burning/ frostbite like feeling in the hands, arms, etc, loss of tactile function, as well as localized swelling in my situation (i have photos) that takes days to subside, even if/ when you stop using the phone. There is also a steady drainage of the battery as this occurs which causes the phone to not function as it should in terms of charge time (but that is a non-concern in comparison) . It also gets extremely hot. Apple refuses to acknowledge the issue and claims it is static electricity when you first complain. If you pursue the issue they continue to deny it is happening even though employees at the Apple Store (and many other individuals) can feel it happening with the defective devices. My first phone to do this was eventually replaced when it became such a problem that it started creating errors in the phones function. It was replaced with the same model, and the new one does exactly the same. When reported to Apple i was told it cant happen, especially twice, despite my first device being replaced for exactly this issue. Apple customer support refuses to acknowledge the issue, except for those who will say it is an accepted issue within their threshold of risk. The associated risk of having electricity transfer from my phone to my body in a way that causes discomfort and tactile problems should be zero. Their solution is to purchase a heavier case or a different model or brand of phone. I shouldnt have to purchase an accessory or anything else to not be hurt by my phone. Especially when I am already using a silicone case from Apple, a glass screen protector, and their mag safe charging system with a surge protector for extra caution. This has been happening since receiving my first of this model in January 2024 and is currently still happening. My first phone was replaced on May 27th 2024. It should also be noted that this problem does not fall under their limited warranty, as per customer service.

incidents.incident_description: My husband and I bought a brand newly built house in June 2023 that came with a new Frigidaire dishwasher. [Product identification tag shows manufacturer as Electrolux Home Products, Inc., Charlotte, NC 28262; Serial # TH30978187; Model # FFID2426TS6A]. We began using the new dishwasher starting at the end of August 2023 when we moved into the house. We regularly smelled an odor of burning plastic when using the dishwasher but could never identify the root cause, which was not evident. In the past 7 to 10 or 12 days, the dishwasher began leaking from the base of it when operating. We tried to troubleshoot and were unable to determine the cause. Today, our home's builder came out to help troubleshoot the dishwasher. He found that water was leaking from the dishwasher when it was operating, and observed water falling on the floor (after the dishwasher's front low kick plate was removed). After further testing, the builder and I noticed that one section of the heating element inside the dishwasher at the base of the appliance, was touching and in direct contact with the dishwasher's interior plastic in one section, had melted the plastic, and the heating element was fused to the plastic. This is a very dangerous condition and could have caused a fire. As it is, the leaking water from the dishwasher, has caused water damage to a section of our new home's hardwood floors, causing a section of the floor to swell up, lift, and separate from other boards. With our Builder, we cut off the power to the dishwasher and the water supply line and have stopped using the dishwasher effective today and henceforth. This Frigidaire brand dishwasher manufactured by Electrolux Home Products, is a danger anywhere it has been sold. My husband did a [REDACTED] search today after we discovered this issue, and found that Electrolux was sued under a class action in U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina on or around November 15, 2012 by lead Plaintiffs [REDACTED] and that, "...Electrolux designed, manufactured, and marketed dishwashers...that contain a serious and dangerous defect, putting many of its customers in harm's way." As consumers with no prior knowledge, ownership or use of a Frigidaire dishwasher prior to purchasing this new house in June 2023, we are shocked that there is prior legal precedent about dangerous Electrolux dishwashers from 12 years ago.

incidents.incident_description: Within 6 months of installing the detectors in his home, they began giving false alarms. The consumer contacted the manufacturer to report his concerns. The manufacturer’s recommendation was to clean the detectors, but they did not instruct how they should be cleaned.The consumer saw that a different manufacturer’s brand, recommended to take theirs apart to blow out the smoke chambers. He tried that with the ones he owns and still had the same problem. The consumer consulted his local fire department and one of the firemen suggested that he vacuum them. He purchased a product that enabled him to vacuum them, but that did not address the problem. Even after vacuuming the detectors, the continued giving false alarms. The frequency of the false alarms varies. Sometimes, a few months will pass before they alarm and in other cases, this can happen every few days.Sometime the detectors will alarm and by the time he reaches the detector, they will cease alarming. However, the issue has become more frequent lately.He spent $650 to purchase 10 of these detectors. He plans to purchase a different brand of detectors for around $1200.

incidents.incident_description: I would like to report Kidde Smoke/CO Alarm with Voice and Wireless (model P40 10DCSCO-W). We had 7 detectors installed by our electrician around November 2023 after a recent home addition. Ever since installation, we have had near weekly false alarms. I followed instructions for possible interference (bad placement and/or needing to spray with compressed air). Nothing worked. After a week in September 2024 of 2-3 false alarms per day (often at 2am), I finally disabled the the 2-3 devices I though may be offending. Other neighbors have reported issues with these or similar alarms since this style of detector is required by County code as part of any permitted home improvements. Reviews on the Kidde website report similar experiences and 1 star reviews. While I fortunately cannot speak to whether these alarms identify true positives with fires (or CO2), I believe the false alarms create a safety issue by inuring or desensitizing consumers in to thinking alarms are not alerting them to and actual fire/CO2 or other unsafe event.

incidents.incident_description: 10/6/2024: The washer became stuck in the drain cycle. He can hear the vacuum motor, but the washer will not move. He tripped the breaker for a few minutes, unplugged the washer and plugged it back into the wall outlet. When he turned the washer back on, it was stuck on that same cycle. He then repeated those steps for approximately 15 - 20 minutes, but the washer was still stuck. If this was left unattended, the washer’s motor could run continuously and possible lead to a fire. When he first noticed the issue, he had no idea how long it was stuck on that cycle. However, he started his last load of clothes nearly 2 hours prior to discovering the issue. 10/7/2024: He called the manufacturer’s Customer Service Number. Their rep. told him that they could send a technician out for $119.00 to diagnose the issue. The consumer noted that he did not want to pay for this repair, because he did not cause it, and the machine was purchased last year. He asked to speak with a higher authority. He was told that he would be directed to their Escalations Department but was not able to speak with a person. incidents.incident_description: Upon wiping the bottom of our Frigidaire double convection oven to clean up a small spill, I realized that the oven enamel was coming off of the oven cavity. The product was being used normally as a typical oven user would. It is unclear to us whether we could have possibly ingested oven enamel due to this issue. We bought a condo which included a Bosch Side by Side, built in refrigerator and ice maker. The prior owner bought the unit new and never occupied it, so the refrigerator was turned on, but never used in day-to-day service. The problem I am reporting is that the ceramic water line to the ice maker has disintegrated, causing minute ceramic debris particles to flow into the water that is becoming ice. The ice is unusable and unsafe. The line is surrounded by foam insulation from the manufacturer, so it is not accessible and cannot be replaced. The disintegration of the line is a defect that was not caused by misuse. There is no access to the line and no situation of operating use of the line that could cause line to fracture and disintegrate the way it did. The problem was discovered by an independent repair technician. The problem was masked by other defects in the freezer, which included a disconnected (severed) wire that should have powered a fan in the freezer. Because the fan did not work, the ice maker never functioned because there is a temperature controller that prevents operation of the ice maker when the ambient temperature in the freezer exceeds a preset temperature. A BSH approved servicer attempted to repair the fan problem and after several unsuccessful repair attempts, declared the unit to be not serviceable. I sought a replacement of the refrigerator. Bosch advised me that the unit was out of warranty, but they would offer me $1,484.85 against the purchase of a new $9,899 replacement unit. Since the replacement unit cost and installation far exceeds BSH offer, I sought an independent repair. That repair person was able to fix the wiring issue and restore normal fan function, but then discovered that the ceramic water line was disintegrating and that it could not be replaced and represented a safety hazard as pieces broke off and flowed into the ice. We have not used the ice and so have not been injured, but anyone with this refrigerator and this problem would not know that foreign bodies are flowing into the ice and so this is a danger to consumers. I have other Bosch products, and have a Bosch refrigerator in another dwelling, and typically Bosch makes a quality product. I am confounded by how this issue happened and why this refrigerator presented with problems that neither repair person had seen in their careers.

The fire went out on it's own, but the red "Hot Surface" indicator light remained on (while surface was not hot) until I pulled the oven out and unplugged it from the outlet. This was extremely frightening to my youngest daughter and me. We were both shocked at how sudden and ferociously the fire started and are relieved that no one was seriously hurt enough to require medical attention. I see that other consumers reported the almost identical issue with this same model with more serious consequences. I found a recall (number 24-335) which included other Samsung models - again, almost identical situations - but my model (NE59J7630SG/AA) was not included in the recall.

incidents.company_comment: (1/10/2025) Delta Faucet Company: Liberty has reached out to this consumer to gather more details in order to fully investigate this report. While Liberty regrets that the consumer had this experience, it does not believe the shower doors it sells pose a significant consumer risk, notwithstanding the fact that because they are glass, they may be broken during the course of use. Tempered glass doors are extremely strong and are commonly used in bathrooms in place of shower curtains. These doors are made to the strict standards of ANSI Z97.1 and CPSC regulations for architectural glass found at 16 CFR part 1201. The tempering process creates stresses on the glass that allow the glass to withstand greater than normal forces on its surface. Tempered glass, although extremely strong, can break if an end or corner is scratched, damaged, or impacted – these types of things can occur when the glass shower door unit is not installed as directed in the instructions provided with the product at the time of sale. It is uncommon for tempered glass to break, but when it happens, the glass does not splinter into jagged shards; rather, it breaks into small granular chunks to minimize risk to nearby people and property. Liberty takes product safety seriously and encourages all consumers to reach out to share information regarding product performance.

After I got up, I saw that the leg of the chair had cracked and it was only held together by what appears to be light glue (no screw or other reinforcement). We only had these dining chairs for a little over a year (purchased November 2023) and we do not use them everyday or stand on them, they are only used for their intended purpose. After this incident I had a lot of back pain and my elbow was very bruised and sore, I thought I might have had a fracture but did not (confirmed with a doctor), however this could have been much much worse which is why I want to report it. I also want to mention that this product on the IKEA website says it is tested at 243 pounds, but I am less than that. I hope this can help get this product off the market as I feel it is not safe.

incidents.incident_description: GE over the range microwave, model JVM7195EF1ES. I was reheating lunch and put 1 minute on the timer. I walked out of the room for about 2 minutes. When I returned the microwave said "START 00:13" and was humming. The microwave carousel was off and the light was off, but the magnetron was still engaged heating the food. I pressed cancel and the clock started showing the time, but the magnetron was still humming. I opened the door and the magnetron stopped. I closed the door and the magnetron started again and the food started to sizzle. The microwave control panel is not turned on (it just shows the time), there is no program set or running, the interior light is off, and the carousel is not turning. Even the fan that cools the magnetron is not running; only the magnetron is active. It can be confirmed that the magnetron is engaged by putting food in the microwave and closing the door. The magnetron, and only the magnetron, will turn on and heat the food. Pressing cancel has no effect. Opening the door turns off the magnetron, but it turns back on when you close the door. This is a FIRE HAZARD as the microwave has failed in an "ON" state. I have unplugged the microwave and will replace it with a different manufacturer's appliance as I don't trust GE any longer (failed ice maker and water solenoid in the GE refrigerator, failed wash pump, control board, touchpad, door sensor, and drain pump in the GE dishwasher (all different years over 8 years), and now a stuck on magnetron in the GE microwave). I really don't trust GE appliances and their reliability.

incidents.company_comment: (6/4/2025) World Kitchen, LLC: This is a response on behalf of Corelle Brands d/b/a World Kitchen to CPSC consumer Report ID: 20250518-58F07-2147331232, regarding a glass baking dish, which the consumer identified as being a Pyrex 9x13 baking dish manufactured by Corelle Brands. The consumer reported that the baking dish broke while it was sitting on the counter next to a heating stove. It does not appear that the consumer has reached out to Corelle Brands directly. The consumer has not submitted the glassware for inspection. If the consumer wishes to do so, Corelle’s Consumer Affairs Department can be reached at support@corellebrands.com or 1-800-999-3436. Based upon Corelle Brands’ review of the proposed records, Corelle Brands responds as follows: I. CORELLE BRANDS’ 16 C.F.R. 1102.12 COMMENTS ON THE REPORTED CONSUMER COMPLAINT. A. Identification and Inspection of the Products at Issue Not Performed Corelle Brands has not had the opportunity to inspect or otherwise view the product at issue in this claim. Often, similar products manufactured by other entities are improperly identified as Corelle Brands products. Without having the opportunity to inspect the baking dish, Corelle Brands is unable to determine whether the product involved in this incident is, in fact, an Corelle Brands product. In addition, because the baking dish has not been provided, Corelle Brands cannot do an inspection as to any potential defect, for common misuse, retailer mishandling, or other cause of the failure. Without an opportunity to review the facts and products involved in the records disclosed, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem. B. Compliance with Industry Standard Corelle Brands’ glass bakeware is manufactured in compliance with the applicable industry standard set forth in Chapter 24 of the Cookware Manufacturing Association Engineering Standards for Cookware and Bakeware. C. Consumer or Retailer Misuse In Corelle Brands’ experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturer’s instructions, and supplier and/or retailer mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide. Examples of this type of mishandling are: hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; retailer mishandling including improper stacking or storage; or using in a too-hot oven. Corelle Brands believes there is a chance either retailer or consumer misuse caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product. D. Tempered Glass Bakeware According to the consumer, they were using a Pyrex 9"x13" glass baking dish. While the stove was being heated, the Pyrex dish was on the counter next to it. At some point, the dish “exploded” and “glass was everywhere” and numerous small shards of glass were noted as being present. There is an explanation for this method of failure. Corelle Brands’ glass bakeware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening. Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury. The method of failure is actually a safety feature rather than evidence of a defect. Therefore, the consumer’s report of the product shattering into many pieces is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass, rather than evidence of a defect. To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for oven bakeware state the following warnings: “Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns. Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.” Glass bakeware is not without limitations. While it is a healthier alternative to other types of bakeware, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break. Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Corelle Brands, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking. Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin. Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority. Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manner—i.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shards—is a priority. Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals. Corelle Brands is proud that it has never had any of its products recalled by the Consumer Product Safety Commission. II. VERIFICATION OF INFORMATION CONTAINED IN COMMENTS AND REQUEST FOR PUBLICATION Pursuant to 16 CFR § 1102.12(c)(3), Corelle Brands verifies that it has reviewed the report of harm and Corelle Brands’ comments related to the report of harm and that the information contained in the comments is true and accurate to the best of Corelle Brands’ knowledge, information, and belief. Pursuant to 16 CFR § 1102.12(c)(4), Corelle Brands requests that the Commission publish the comment in the Database, and consents to the publication of the comment in the Database. Thank you for the opportunity to respond.

incidents.incident_description: Not long after I bought a Whirlpool range, Model # WEFES333ORZO (06/22/2025), I reported this stove as dangerous. The inside of the bottom drawer (where you "pull it out") is "unfinished" and the edges extremely sharp. My fear is for a child or someone older (with thinner skin) to pull out the drawer (a standard function of a drawer!). Tonight, I had a pan "splatter screen" fall out of the drawer and "inside" the stove. When I reached in to pull it out, I cut my wrist (drawing blood) on the edge of the back of the drawer. Had it been a sliver, bit deeper, I may well have bled to death before 911 could get here! On August 26, 2025, I arrived at my office and heard a constant beeping from our Kidde carbon monoxide and smoke alarm, model number P40110DCSC0. There was no fire, and the smoke alarm was stored in its original box without being used. The smoke alarm was stored in an air-conditioned office building. I contacted the manufacturer to report this issue. The smoke alarm was manufactured in July 2019. The manufacturer informed me that they would not replace the failed smoke alarm because it had not been activated within a year of its manufacture. They also stated that the battery would drain faster when the alarm is in the standby (off) position if not used. According to them, the battery would last longer if the alarm were used, which does not make sense given that these smoke alarms are designed to be interconnected wirelessly to multiple smoke alarms and cannot be recharged. This is a significant issue for consumers' safety and a false sense of security, as the battery does not last 10 years, even when in standby mode. The manufacturer offered no replacement or support and placed the blame on the consumer for not turning it on.
incidents.company_comment: (9/17/2025) UTC Fire & Security : At Kidde we take residential fire safety very seriously, which is why all of our products are designed to comply with the rigorous standards set by Underwriters Laboratories for performance and reliability. Nuisance alarms are a rare but possible occurrence, and have numerous potential causes that do not relate in any way to a defect in the product. We note that alarms must be cleaned on a regular basis to keep them free of dust and debris, in accordance with the instructions in the user manual. They must also be placed away from vents and fans, as instructed by the user manual. Improper maintenance or placement are often the cause of such false alarms. We also note that this particular unit was used as a demonstration unit by the fire department, not as a conventional alarm device. This nonconventional use may have contributed to the nuisance alarming. We are in contact with this consumer, and have agreed to replace their unit free of charge, despite being out of warranty, and we will retrieve the existing unit for further examination in our testing laboratory.

incidents.incident_description: Product Involved: Whirlpool WFE540H0ES Electric Range Oven Incident Date: 09/06/2025 Location: [REDACTED], Colorado On the evening of 09/06/2025, I was using my Whirlpool WFE540H0ES electric range oven to bake food when a dangerous incident occurred. While the oven was operating at a regular baking temperature, I suddenly saw a bright orange flame inside the oven, accompanied by loud crackling and popping noises similar to a welding arc. Within seconds, sparks began flying throughout the interior of the oven. The food inside was untouched and not burned, which indicates that the source of the problem came from the oven itself, not the food or any spills. While this was happening, the bottom of the oven began to melt, and a hole approximately 2 inches by 1 inch burned completely through the metal base of the oven cavity. I immediately attempted to turn off the oven using the control panel, but the entire display panel shut down on its own, and the oven powered off suddenly. Despite the shutdown, flames continued to burn briefly inside before eventually extinguishing on their own. The fire produced heavy, acrid, chemical-smelling smoke that quickly filled the house and triggered all of our smoke detectors. Out of caution, we switched off the breaker manually, though the circuit breaker did not trip automatically despite the severity of the incident. While there were no burns or direct physical injuries, the heavy smoke exposure caused health issues for multiple members of the household: Both my husband and I experienced significant respiratory irritation, resulting in frequent coughing and throat discomfort. The strong odor and harsh fumes caused headaches for my husband and 3 year old daughter the following morning.

This is what I have typed up to email to attorneys. Can you tell me if this is good or not? On Tuesday evening, my 10-year-old nonverbal son with Down Syndrome and Autism nearly severed his fingers with a Ninja Blast portable blender. I had bought it a year ago to make smoothies for my mother after her stroke, but she passed away before I had a chance to even use it. My kitchen is under renovation, so my appliances are all out of their normal place. This blender hasn't been out of the cabinet in a year, so when my son saw it, I assume it caught his interest, being new to him. I was preparing his evening medication with him standing beside me, and within an instant, he had picked up the blender and simultaneously turned on the blades with his hand inside. It happened so fast I couldn't even register what was happening. To my knowledge, it hadn't even been charged in the past year as it has been stored away in the cabinet. It did not have the lid on, so I also did not understand how the motor could turn on. Seven extremely traumatic hours later, two ER sedations and stitches, I arrived back home at 3am and crawled into bed to try to make sense of what happened. In my research, I discovered that this particular model lacks a safety latch to prevent the blades from turning on when the lid is open. Every blender and Ninja I have ever owned did. I am absolutely devastated that this happened to my son. He has endured so much in his life...being born with Down Syndrome and a heart condition, being adopted from China at 3, heart repair resulting in pulmonary hypertension at 4, epilepsy, leukemia at 7, which he fought bravely and is now in remission. He already has so much medical trauma that it is almost impossible to even succeed at basic well-child care for him. This should have never happened.

I use a Conair 1875 Styler to blow dry my hair every morning. Ive owned this unit for approximately four years. I have short hair which requires less than a minute of drying time every day. This morning after about 15 seconds of use, the unit stopped working. About 4 seconds later, it began running again, so I continued using it for a few more seconds when it shut off again on its own. As I held it away from my head, the unit made a loud popping sound. Simultaneously, it sent out a burst of orange flames, sparks, and smoke. I immediately threw the unit in my sink and unplugged it from the wall. Oddly, it never tripped my GFI outlet, and the outlet is working fine. This Conair Styler has never been dropped or abused. Im the sole user. Every day, I pull it from the drawer where I store it, use it briefly, then set it back in the drawer. The outlet its plugged into is 7 years old and was installed when my home was built in 2018. The Conair Styler shows no signs of having an explosive incident. It still looks brand new. If I had been holding the u it closer to my head when it shot out flames, I undoubtedly would have been seriously burned.

None of the pictures or recipes included elude to the fact the blade is sharp enough to handle meat. Excersize care when handling blade under before first use does not explain clearly why. Are we Excersizing care to avoid damage of product? Again #3 blade being sharp. Does not say or illustrate the severity of sharpness. Even giving a warning of lacerations. While making a small fruit smoothie in a Ninja blender purchased from Costco, the product violently failed during normal use. The blade assembly suddenly ejected from the container with explosive force. The loud noise was so strong that it caused ear pain, and the smoothie contents sprayed across the kitchen, covering walls, counters, and floors. The blender was being used properly with fruit, ice, and liquid, nothing unusual or outside of normal use. In fact, I have blended much harsher items in the past (such as frozen bananas) without issue, so there is no reason this smoothie should have caused such a catastrophic failure. The unit was operated by an adult following normal instructions. The flying blade scratched my kitchen floors, and the splattered contents permanently stained my walls and wood surfaces, leaving damage that will require resurfacing and repainting. Although I was fortunate not to be physically struck, the blade assembly launched out at high speed directly toward the area where I was standing. It could easily have cut my hands, face, or even my neck and caused life-threatening injury. The sudden blast was loud enough to cause temporary ear discomfort. The incident created significant property damage and could have easily resulted in hospitalization or worse had the blade struck me. The product has since been returned to Costco, which issued a refund and documented the incident, but this dangerous malfunction needs to be formally reported for consumer safety.

On May 9, 2023, my son had just turned ten months old. That same day, while playing in a fully padded, age-appropriate play area under my supervision, he suffered a life-threatening traumatic brain injury caused by the Fisher-Price Linkimals Cool Beats Penguin Baby & Toddler Learning Toy with Music & Lights. Because of his height and early mobility, traditional pack-and-play yards were unstable. We created a safe, low-to-the-ground play space with extra padding so he could safely practice standing and cruising. The Cool Beats Penguin toy was clearly labeled for ages 9 months and up, giving me every reason to believe it was safe for his developmental stage. Shortly after returning home from shopping, I placed my son in his play yard with this toy. While cruising and taking steps, he lost his balance and fell onto the toy, striking his head against the toys hard plastic beak or foot. Within seconds, he began convulsing. My ten-month-old baby was having a seizure. We immediately called 911 and rushed him to the emergency room. After imaging, doctors discovered bleeding in his brain and rushed him into emergency surgery (craniotomy) to relieve pressure and remove the clot. They later confirmed the impact was consistent with blunt-force trauma from a hard object. This toy is marketed for infants just learning to sit, crawl, and stand yet its construction includes sharp-angled, rigid plastic components that act like impact weapons in the hands or under the weight of a baby. There were no warnings, disclaimers, or visible cautions alerting parents to the risk of skull injury or blunt-force trauma. The age labeling and marketing gave a false sense of safety that nearly cost my child his life. Fisher-Price has a long history of product recalls tied to infant injuries and deaths. It is unconscionable that a toy designed for babies would be engineered with hard plastic edges at head level for a cruising infant. This is not an isolated parental oversight it is a design flaw that violates basic safety expectations for toys marketed to infants under one year old. Because of this product, my son endured emergency brain surgery before his first birthday. No family should ever have to live that nightmare. I am submitting this report to request a full safety investigation into the Fisher-Price Linkimals Cool Beats Penguin toy and to urge the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission to assess whether this product meets infant-toy impact-safety standards. A 10-month-old should not have to survive a craniotomy because of a toy labeled safe for babies.

incidents.incident_description: We purchased a Samsung Family Hub refrigerator in February 2025. Since installation, the refrigerator has had multiple serious safety and performance issues. The refrigerator is electrically unsafe. On multiple occasions, family members have experienced electric shock when touching the refrigerator or freezer doors. The refrigerator doors create a pinch hazard. My childs fingers have repeatedly gotten stuck when closing the door, creating a serious risk of injury to a child. The freezer does not function properly. At times, all frozen food completely melts. At other times, food becomes freezer burned due to unstable temperatures. The freezer does not maintain a consistent safe temperature. Food repeatedly melts and then refreezes, causing freezer burn. This has caused repeated food loss. This has resulted in spoiled food and food waste on multiple occasions, and we have had to throw away food many times due to unsafe storage conditions. This appears to be a temperature control failure and presents a food safety risk. The top of the refrigerator shakes excessively every time the door is opened, which raises concerns about internal mechanical or electrical failure. This product presents an ongoing safety hazard to my child and my family. I have contacted the retailer multiple times requesting a return or refund due to safety risk, but they refused and told me to use warranty service only. This is not a minor repair issue but a dangerous appliance. The hazard is ongoing. My childs fingers and my own fingers continue to get stuck every time we open or close the refrigerator door and drawers. This occurs repeatedly during normal use. This is not a one-time incident. It happens daily and presents a continuous risk of finger injury to a child. Because of this ongoing pinch hazard my child and I continue to experience finger pinch incidents when opening and closing the doors and drawers and repeated incidents during normal use. This is an ongoing hazard, not a one-time event. This appliance is unsafe for continued use in our home. These issues together make the refrigerator unsafe for continued use in a household with a child.

incidents.incident_description: I, [REDACTED], am submitting this form and acting as the representative of the victim [REDACTED]. I purchased a Kidde combination smoke and explosive gas detector from Home Depot in Atlanta a few months ago. About a month after installing it, I accidentally left my gas on for around 15 minutes. incidents.company_comment: (3/3/2026) UTC Fire & Security : At Kidde we take residential fire safety very seriously, which is why all of our products comply with the rigorous standards set by Underwriters Laboratories for performance and reliability. Below is our latest response to this consumer. We are replacing their unit and retrieving it for testing in our labs to ensure that it is working as intended. As you will see from the explanation below, it is quite likely that the unit did not alarm because gas did not accumulate above threshold levels set by UL standards for this type of product, rather than as a result of a defect. We will confirm through testing in our lab. "[REDACTED] Thank you for reaching out and for taking the time to describe your experience. I understand how concerning it must have been to smell gas in your home and not see any response from your Kidde combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector. We take issues involving life safety devices very seriously, and I appreciate the opportunity to address your concerns. Why the Alarm May Not Have Activated Based on the User Guide for the Kidde KN COEG 3 (see attached), the unit functions as both a carbon monoxide (CO) alarm and an explosive gas detector, but each works in specific ways: Carbon monoxide detection: CO is only produced when fuel is burning incompletely, not when unburned natural gas is accidentally released. A gas stove left on without ignition releases natural gas, which contains no carbon monoxide. Therefore, a CO reading of zero is expected in this situation. Explosive gas detection: The unit is also designed to detect natural gas or propane. When it senses either gas at hazardous concentrations, the display shows “GAS” and the alarm emits a repeating pattern (½ second beep / ½ second silence). However, the manual also notes that the alarm is intended to function as a monitor, not a rapid response device for very short term or low level gas presence: [[REDACTED]] “This CO and Gas alarm is designed to act as a monitor. It is not designed for use as a short term…” In many cases, a small or brief release of natural gas may dissipate too quickly or remain below the alarm’s threshold, even though the odorant (mercaptan) is detectable to your nose at extremely low levels. Why You Smelled Gas but No Alarm Occurred Natural gas companies add a strong-smelling odorant so leaks are identifiable at levels far below dangerous concentrations. Your detector, however, must reach a specific threshold before triggering to avoid constant nuisance alarms. This model’s carbon monoxide (CO) alarm is designed to activate only after CO has been present at certain levels for a specific amount of time. Here’s what that means in everyday terms: At 70 parts per million (ppm): The alarm will sound if this level continues for about 1 to 4 hours. At 150 ppm: The alarm will sound within 10 to 50 minutes at this higher level. At 400 ppm: This is a dangerous level, and the alarm will go off within 4 to 15 minutes. What this really means for you Carbon monoxide alarms are intentionally designed not to go off right away at low levels. This helps prevent unnecessary false alarms from minor or short lived CO fluctuations. Instead, these alarms follow national safety standards to alert you only when CO reaches levels known to cause harm if exposure continues. The higher the CO level, the faster the alarm responds: Low level = slower response Medium level = faster response High level = very fast response This timing helps make sure you’re alerted when it truly matters for your health and safety. In short, it is possible to clearly smell gas without reaching the alarm threshold, and the device may still be functioning correctly. Next Steps & Recommended Resolution Even with the explanations above, your concern is completely valid—any uncertainty around a safety device warrants attention. Since you suspect a defect, and because your attempt to obtain support from Kidde was unsuccessful, we want to ensure you’re taken care of properly. Here’s what I can do for you: We will replace the unit to ensure you have full confidence in your home’s safety equipment. You should receive the replacement unit in 7-10 business days. Additionally, I would like to collect the unit that you believe did not function properly for analysis. Please find attached a return shipping label so that you can send that unit to us. Additional Safety Note If you ever smell gas again—regardless of what any detector shows—Kidde’s official guidance is to evacuate immediately, avoid operating electric switches, and contact your fire department. We sincerely appreciate you bringing this to our attention. Your safety is our priority, and we want you to feel fully protected and supported. Please reply with your preferred shipping address, and I will arrange for your replacement unit right away."

incidents.incident_description: I am submitting a safety complaint regarding an LG gas double oven purchased new from Home Depot at the end of 2016 (Model: LDG4313ST). At present, we do not feel it is safe to operate this appliance in our home. The unit remains unusable, and our household has incurred ongoing disruption and expense while awaiting a safe resolution. Historical Issues Experienced: - At one point, the bottom oven was shooting visible flames beyond normal operation. LG Support sent a technician and the issue was addressed. - We later experienced electrical failures with the top oven, including shorting out, tripping breakers, and causing a failure at the wall outlet, which required an electrician to replace the outlet due to damage. - Subsequently, the top oven stopped functioning altogether and began causing interference and operational issues with the bottom oven. - On Christmas Eve of this year, the bottom oven failed completely, leaving our household without a working oven during the holidays. Tempered glass doors are extremely strong and are commonly used in bathrooms in place of shower curtains. These doors are made to the strict standards of ANSI Z97.1 and CPSC regulations for architectural glass found at 16 CFR part 1201. The tempering process creates stresses on the glass that allow the glass to withstand greater than normal forces on its surface. Tempered glass, although extremely strong, can break if an end or corner is scratched, damaged, or impacted – these types of things can occur when the glass shower door unit is not installed as directed in the instructions provided with the product at the time of sale. It is uncommon for tempered glass to break, but when it happens, the glass does not splinter into jagged shards; rather, it breaks into small granular chunks to minimize risk to nearby people and property. incidents.incident_description: The day prior to the incident, staff member A recalls seeing the message ERR on the microwave display. Staff member A reports pressing the cancel button and the message disappeared with no further incident. On the day of the incident the majority of the staff in this small office had ordered in tacos to celebrate taco Tuesday. As such, the only reported use of the microwave was by one individual in the early morning to heat oatmeal. No other use was reported. As staff member A entered the kitchen to retrieve her lunch, she noted the microwave was making a noise like it does when typically operating. Staff member A reported no food in the microwave and the message PF on the display screen. She pressed the button to open the door and the message disappeared. Staff member A left the door in the open position and exited the kitchen. An unknown time later, staff member B entered the kitchen to retrieve a snack from the refrigerator adjacent to the microwave. Staff member B reported that she almost hit her head on the now open microwave door. Subsequently, she shut the door to the microwave, retrieved her snack and exited the kitchen. An unknown time later, staff member C entered the kitchen where staff members D and E were sat at the table eating their lunch. While walking in, the three staff reported hearing what they described as an explosion and a loud pop followed by seeing dark smoke rolling out of the inside of the microwave. Additionally, a plastic food splash guard that was stored on top of the microwave became airborne and landed approximately 4 feet from the microwave. Staff member C responded by closing the door to the microwave while staff member D retrieved a fire extinguisher, and staff member E called 911. Staff member C took the fire extinguisher from staff member D and reopened the door. Upon doing so she reported additional smoke inside the microwave. Upon deploying the fire extinguisher staff member C recalls seeing flame present behind the perforations in the inside of the microwave behind the control panel. The fire department arrived and took the microwave outside. Once outside the firefighters noticed flames in the same inside area of the microwave behind the control panel. They used water to extinguish the flames. The fire departments investigation team was on scene to document the incident.

I am filing this complaint regarding a Whirlpool dryer purchased from Lowes on September 20, 2025, for over 700.00 including tax. Model # WED5010LW1 - Serial# ME3689248. The dryer is still well within the manufacturers one-year warranty period. On May 3, 2026, the dryer suddenly stopped heating and began producing a strong burning smell during operation. Upon removing the back panel, we discovered burned wiring and evidence of significant electrical failure. Due to the obvious fire hazard, the dryer was immediately unplugged and taken out of service. Whirlpool dispatched a technician from [REDACTED] out of Lexington, Kentucky, to inspect the appliance. During the service visit, the technician advised that there had been a major failure within the dryer and stated they could not determine what component failed first or what specifically caused the failure. I was further informed that multiple major electrical components would require replacement. When I questioned why Whirlpool would not simply replace a less-than-one-year-old appliance that experienced a severe electrical malfunction and potential fire hazard, the technician stated that he personally agreed replacement would make more sense, but that the decision was Whirlpools to make. Whirlpool, however, stated they would only authorize repair if the technician deemed the unit repairable. This response is unacceptable given the circumstances. This was not a minor mechanical issue. This was a significant electrical failure involving burned wiring and an unexplained overheating event inside an appliance operating within my home. Even Whirlpools own authorized technician could not identify the root cause of the failure. That creates a serious safety concern because there is no assurance the same unidentified failure could not occur again after repair. I purchased a new Whirlpool appliance because I trusted the brands quality and safety standards. I do not believe consumers should be expected to continue using an appliance that experienced a major electrical malfunction with burned wiring, especially when the exact cause of failure cannot be determined. The potential risk of future electrical fire or property damage is deeply concerning. I am requesting that Whirlpool replace the dryer rather than attempt piecemeal repairs to a unit that suffered a major unexplained electrical failure within the warranty period. I believe replacement is the only reasonable resolution that adequately addresses both consumer safety concerns and product reliability expectations.

incidents.incident_description: I am reporting a serious safety incident involving a Pyrex glass casserole/baking dish that suddenly exploded after being removed from the oven and placed on my kitchen countertop. The product being used was a Pyrex glass casserole dish/bakeware dish. I was using it in a normal household kitchen setting to cook food in the oven. After baking, I removed the hot casserole dish from the oven and placed it on my countertop. Shortly after it was placed on the counter, the glass dish violently shattered/exploded without warning. Glass fragments/shrapnel launched across the kitchen. My two young children were nearby at the time, and the glass shrapnel launched in their direction. This created an immediate and serious risk of lacerations, eye injury, burns, and other injuries. Thankfully, no one was physically injured.Or add: Although no physical injury occurred, this was a near-miss incident that could have seriously injured my children. The dish was being used as ordinary bakeware: placed in the oven for cooking, then removed and placed on a kitchen countertop. I later researched Pyrex product care instructions and found that the company warns consumers not to place hot glass are on cool or wet surfaces and to use a dry cloth, potholder, trivet, or cooling rack. However, this warning was not prominently visible to me on the product packaging or on the dish itself before use. This is especially concerning because many consumers reasonably believe granite/stone countertops are heat safe and would not understand that placing hot Pyrex glassware on a countertop could cause the product to explode or violently shatter. The warning about this hazard should be displayed prominently in large, bold lettering on the packaging and/or directly on the product because the risk is severe and not obvious to ordinary consumers. I am reporting this because the product shattered violently during foreseeable household use and created a serious injury hazard to children and anyone nearby. I believe the product warning is inadequate and not prominent enough given the risk of sudden breakage, flying glass, and serious injury. I request that CPSC review this product and the adequacy of Pyrexs warnings regarding thermal shock, countertop placement, and the risk of glass explosion/shattering. Product details: Brand: Pyrex Product type: Glass casserole/baking dish Approximate size/model: 9x13
incidents.company_comment: (6/4/2026) World Kitchen, LLC: This is a response on behalf of Corelle Brands d/b/a World Kitchen to CPSC consumer Report ID: 20260519-0DBC1-2147319060, regarding a Pyrex 9x13 casserole dish, which the consumer identified as being a Pyrex product manufactured by Corelle Brands. The consumer reported they were using the dish in the oven, removed it, and placed it directly on the countertop. The dish then “violently shattered/exploded.” It does not appear that the consumer has reached out to Corelle Brands directly. The consumer has not submitted the glassware for inspection. If the consumer wishes to do so, Corelle’s Consumer Affairs Department can be reached at support@corellebrands.com or 1-800-999-3436. Based upon Corelle Brands’ review of the proposed records, Corelle Brands responds as follows: I. CORELLE BRANDS’ 16 C.F.R. 1102.12 COMMENTS ON THE REPORTED CONSUMER COMPLAINT. A. Identification and Inspection of the Products at Issue Not Performed Corelle Brands has not had the opportunity to inspect or otherwise view the product at issue in this claim. Often, similar products manufactured by other entities are improperly identified as Corelle Brands products. Without having the opportunity to inspect the container, Corelle Brands is unable to determine whether the product involved in this incident is, in fact, a Corelle Brands product. In addition, because the container has not been provided, Corelle Brands cannot do an inspection as to any potential defect, for common misuse, retailer mishandling, or other cause of the failure. Without an opportunity to review the facts and products involved in the records disclosed, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem. B. Compliance with Industry Standard Corelle Brands’ glass bakeware is manufactured in compliance with the applicable industry standard set forth in Chapter 24 of the Cookware Manufacturing Association Engineering Standards for Cookware and Bakeware. C. Consumer or Retailer Misuse In Corelle Brands’ experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturer’s instructions, and supplier and/or retailer mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide. Examples of this type of mishandling are: hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; retailer mishandling including improper stacking or storage; or using in a too-hot oven. Corelle Brands believes there is a chance either retailer or consumer misuse caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product. D. Tempered Glass Bakeware According to the consumer, the 9x13 dish “exploded” when it was placed on the countertop after being used in the oven. There is an explanation for this method of failure. Corelle Brands glassware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening. Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury. The method of failure is actually a safety feature rather than evidence of a defect. Therefore, the consumer’s report of the product “exploding” is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass, rather than evidence of a defect. To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for oven bakeware state the following warnings: “Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns. Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.” Glass bakeware is not without limitations. While it is a healthier alternative to other types of bakeware, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break. Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Corelle, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking. Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin. Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority. Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manner—i.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shards—is a priority. Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals. II. VERIFICATION OF INFORMATION CONTAINED IN COMMENTS AND REQUEST FOR PUBLICATION Pursuant to 16 CFR § 1102.12(c)(3), Corelle Brands verifies that it has reviewed the report of harm and Corelle Brands’ comments related to the report of harm and that the information contained in the comments is true and accurate to the best of Corelle Brands’ knowledge, information, and belief. Pursuant to 16 CFR § 1102.12(c)(4), Corelle Brands requests that the Commission publish the comment in the Database, and consents to the publication of the comment in the Database. Thank you for the opportunity to respond.

On June 20th, I was sleeping in my basement when I woke up to smoke and the smell of burning plastic. I noticed that my 2016 Samsung 50-inch TV (Model UN50J6200AFXZA) was smoldering in the bottom-left corner. I immediately unplugged the TV to prevent further risk or damage. As a combat veteran diagnosed with chronic PTSD, I often sleep with the TV on for background noise. I had set the TV to turn off after two hours of use, but this did not happen. The screen was blank, yet I could still hear the sound from the channel. I have heard about multiple similar incidents involving various Samsung models, which motivated me to create this report. After contacting Samsung, they requested physical proof that I had removed the label with the model and serial number. Samsung offered me a refund of approximately 10% (around $50). While this was a nice gesture, the core issue remains unaddressed. I am concerned that someone could lose their home, become injured, or, even worse, lose their life due to this problem. Thank you for your concern

My LG electric range, model number LREL6323S, has a burner that repeatedly overheats while I am cooking food on it. While an electric cooktop, burner should cycle on and off depending on the setting level, this one will occasionally and unexpectedly cycle on and remain on indefinitely. This has ruined many food items and a few pots and pans. However, on one occasion it overheated a pan of oil, which began smoking so much that it was apparent that it would soon catch fire. It was serviced once under warranty, but that did not solve the problem. During my research into the problem, I observed on several platforms that many consumers are reporting the very same problem with LG ranges and I learned that the issue is caused by a faulty element control switch (part number EBF62174907), which was what was replaced during the warranty service mentioned above. While I searched multiple appliance parts sites, I noticed that many of them listed that part as the most commonly purchased part for LG electric ranges. Clearly, this range model and any other model that uses this control part is a fire hazard. The approximate occurrence date I am providing is just the first of several (hundreds) of occurrences. The most recent incident was on 06/26/2026.
